utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, also good afternoon to the Defence. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, and Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and learned friends from the Prosecution. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and, together with Mr. John Jones, I represent the Defence counsel of Mr. Naser Oric. And together with us, our legal assistant, Miss Adisa Mehic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic and good afternoon to you and your team. Are there any preliminaries apart from the fact that I am given advanced notice of problems with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: With a view to this witness, well one might indicate there is problems, but we have a request to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will go into private session, but apart from matters related to this witness, are there any other preliminary matters you would like to raise? None?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, because I understand that the Prosecution has another matter to raise, which is not related strictly speaking to the witness himself. Yes, what is it all about, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours -- and I apologise for the inconvenience that this came up a little bit late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no inconvenience at all, Mr. Wubben. We are managing a case and these things happen all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have revised translations of exhibits P501, 502, 503 and 504 and these are available at the convenience of the parties and they will be handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Can we now go into private session, back to private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's go back to private session, please

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the benefit of the public, that couldn't follow the proceedings till now, we have been dealing in private session, in closed session, certain procedural matters that arose, that needed to be resolved before the witness could start his testimony. The witness has already been sworn in and he is about to be examined in-chief by Madam Patricia Sellers for the Prosecution. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged to ask you to please state your full name for the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were you important in the town of Obadi?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, 1959 in the village of Obadi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you move to the town or hamlet of Bjelovac in 1974?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Not to Voljevica. To Bjelovac. That was in 1974.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And is that in the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please confirm for the Trial Chamber that you have six brothers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have six brothers and three sisters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In 1992, did two or three of your brothers still reside in the town of Obadi in Srebrenica municipality? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Two brothers, father and a cousin who was 16 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in the town of Bjelovac, did you have sisters who resided there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Two sisters and -- two sisters and a brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic [sic] let's go back to 1980 --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Petrovic, can we please go back to 1980, between 1980 and 1992. Would you tell the Trial Chamber where you were working.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: From June 1980, I worked at Srebrenica, at the gas station there. The gas station is at the entrance to Srebrenica, to the right. That's the only gas station in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you work during the day shift or did you work during the night shift at the gas station?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Both the day and the night shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, as someone who worked at the only gas station in Srebrenica for a period of 12 years, did you come to know a lot of people in Srebrenica, in particular, those who had cars or motor vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you have regular customers during that 12-year period?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you speak with people at times even though you might not have known their names?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I spoke with all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you often recognise what ethnic group they were from, either Croat or Muslim or Serb without necessarily knowing their name?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could tell the ethnic background on the basis of how people spoke, the accents, the words they used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, would you consider that you had good relationships with the people who came to the gas station to ask for gas or any other service?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you friendly both to Serbs, Muslims or Croats during your time period that you worked at the gas station?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, with all of them. I had friends, in fact more of my friends were Muslims than Serbs because at that time the town itself had a majority Muslim population. I think about 88 per cent were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did a person named Naser Oric ever come to the gas station while you were working there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just before the war broke out, I think sometime around 1991, maybe early 1992, I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you able, when he was at the gas station, to speak to him on a couple of occasions?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if he came to the gas station and if I served him. I saw him several times. He would stand there at the gas station with his friends, but I did not have any closer contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now what did you know about Naser Oric yourself, other than the fact that he came to the gas station and occasionally got gas?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the arrival in Srebrenica, I had heard that he worked in Belgrade, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Had you heard whether he was an athletic person or an intellectual person or anything else of that nature?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: He was an athletic person. I think that he was in the DB, the State Security in Belgrade. That's what I heard. I'm not sure about it. This was the rumour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see him with a man called Mrki?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I object. That's a very leading question. In fact, there's been a series of questions which have been leading to a greater or lesser degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a direct question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But my learned friend should have said, "Did you see him in company with anyone" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She should have asked him first whether he has ever heard of a person called Mrki. And then she could proceed to ask the witness whether he ever saw Naser, the person he claims to be Naser Oric, with the person he claims to be Mrki, and then we will be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the correct approach really would be to say, "Did you see him alone with others, if with others do you know who those people were, do you know their names."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be taking the slow coach.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well if the witness -- if we wish the witness to have suggested to him he should remember Mrki as being in the company of Naser Oric, as well as others, then that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it the way I suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour might I also state I believe that the witness did testify that he saw him in the company with other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He did say that already. But please ask him whether he has ever heard of a guy called Mrki.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You've heard Your Honour's question. Mr. Petrovic, have you ever heard of a person called Mrki?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the next question is whether he ever saw this -- person he claims to be Naser Oric, with a person he claims to know as Mrki. First in the petrol station. Second, anywhere else for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please ask the question as Your Honour has phrased it, yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did I see Naser Oric before? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No. Did you see him with someone named Mrki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer that question first, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did see him, because they came to the gas station. They hung together. Mrki and he. Mrki was from Voljevica because -- they used to do body building together in the gym in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, Mr. Petrovic, I would also like to ask you, while you were working at the gas station, did you ever see a person known as Zulfo Tursonovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: I do know him. He was from Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to talk to him or see him in your work capacity?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: He would come to the gas station quite often. He would buy gas for cutting wood for the chain saws, because he was -- that's what he was doing. He was also a farmer. And that's why I would see him quite often at the gas station, once a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, were you aware of what type of reputation that Zulfo Tursonovic had in 1992 or prior to that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: He used to be in trouble with his own ethnic group, the Muslims. If I remember it correctly, in a cafe in Srebrenica he had killed some people, some Muslims, and he was, in fact, in prison up until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now would you describe Zulfo Tursonovic as a calm person or a person who was not calm? Who was agitated or had tendencies toward violence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's -- here I will step in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will withdraw the last phrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you know Zulfo Tursonovic well enough to be able to describe to us his character?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And according to you, what was his character? What kind of a person was he? Forget that he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was tall, he had a moustache. He was about two metres tall. Perhaps 1.90 metre to two metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what kind of a character was he? What was his character? His temperament? Was he nice, jovial person, temper mental person? Aggressive person, someone you would keep at a distance? Someone you could mix with without any problems? What -- was he an angry old man? What was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not say that he was aggressive in his behaviour on the basis from what I was able to observe at the gas station. He acted normal, just like any other customer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your knowledge of Zulfo Tursonovic originates only from what you were able to assess and establish at the petrol station, at the entrance of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And not based on any other information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you also know of a person called Akif Ustic, in the capacity of working at the gas station, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, first of all, the physical appearance of Akif Ustic and then explain how you got to know him, if you did.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akif Ustic, I know. He was my P.E. teacher, when I went to school in Sase. And after that I saw him in Srebrenica, where he lived, and in my workplace I saw him almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to get to know the character, the temperament of Akif Ustic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: As a person he was an angry man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you ever have an occasion where Akif Ustic was angry with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Not before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you - turning to 1991 and 1992 - about the political atmosphere in Srebrenica municipality and Bratunac municipality. Could you tell the Trial Chamber if there was, at that time period, any political tension.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: When the parties were established, that's when turbulence started in Srebrenica and Bratunac. Those parties were the SDS and the SDA, and people opted for them. And one could already feel a division between the ethnic groups in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, prior to 1992, did you belong to a political party?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: From 1979 to 1981, I was a member of the League of Communists. And when the new parties were established, I voted for the SDS, but I was never its member.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you attend SDS meetings or were you in any way active with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. I have never been a member of any other political parties and I've never participated in any political meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm now going to move to a slightly different area, when he stops working, but I understand on the transcript it might be unclear, from Mr. Petrovic referred to "P.E.," which I believe is at line 25, and -- page 25, I'm sorry, line 4. Mr. Petrovic, might I ask you, what does P.E. mean? You mentioned Akif Ustic was your teacher in P.E. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what that stands for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's physical exercises.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would use that as an abbreviation for physical education and the witness says he was a teacher of physical -- of physical education, that was the name of that course or subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic, did you stop working at the gas station in 1992 and, if so, what were the circumstances in which you stopped working?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of March, 1992, I don't know the exact date. It might have been the 12th of March. I stopped working in Srebrenica because it was hard for me to get to work. The night guards already started at checkpoints on both sides and it was impossible for me to travel to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the night guards on both sides. Could you be a bit clearer for the Trial Chamber, which sides are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian side and the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you on your way to work one time in Zaluzje?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: One morning, as I set off to work, I was on a bus travelling from Sase to Srebrenica and a bus stop was on Kriva [phoen] road on the border between Zalazje and Bjelovac. It was early in the morning. Some young men were at the stop and they told me not to go back to that stop during the night, because it wasn't safe. That's when I went home and I never returned back to work. The gas station remained open, but it was manned by people from Srebrenica, those who didn't have to commute to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And the people who stopped the bus, were they ethnically Muslims or were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And the people who were on the bus, were they Muslims? Or Serbs? Or was it a mixed ethnic population?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the morning when I got back, I did not see the bus. However, the bus usually carried people of mixed ethnicity or different ethnic groups. They all travelled together on the same bus where I travelled. Those were the people that worked in various companies, the driver was a Muslim, Selko [phoen], and another was Ilko Iljic [phoen]. He was my neighbour. These two men drove the bus that we used to get to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And the piece of territory that you were going through, Zaluzje, was that primarily or predominantly Muslim or Serb territory at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Zaluzje and Voljevica were Muslim villages that I had to pass through in order to get to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you stopped going to work at the gas station, did you then start working in your town, Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no work for me in Bjelovac. I stopped working completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In April 1992, did there come a time when you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would please tell the Trial Chamber what it meant and how it changed your life to be mobilised in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: A list was made of people who would defend the village of Bjelovac. That was the mobilisation. All the able-bodied men were mobilised in April, on the 18th of April, I believe. I may be mistaken. In any case I'm sure of the month; it was April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And those who were supposed to defend Bjelovac, did they form groups or organisations to mount that defence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, until the moment the war started, we had night guards. Just like the other side had. It was just for security purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did the SDS political party participate in the organisation of the night guards?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: The villagers of Bjelovac did that. I suppose they were the SDS. They voted for the SDS, so they could not have been anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you attend any of the sessions or meetings where the organisation was taking place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. I've already told you that I was not involved in any sort of politics. I never attended any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know of a man named Aca who comes from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: A man whose name was Aca turned up in Bjelovac. I didn't know him. He was not from the area. He came to Bjelovac. And he told us that he had been sent from Bratunac in order to restore order to Bjelovac. It was very difficult to force anybody to stand guard. Everybody wanted to stand guard by their own house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was he able to eventually organise a guard in Bjelovac that functioned regularly or militarily?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: He provided some trenches. He told us where the sentry duty would take place, and for a while after that there were guards. We did stand guard for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, as members of the guard, did you receive weapons to use during the guard period?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those persons who were on duty service, who were guards, they carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were these weapons received from Bratunac? Or were they weapons that people had?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Some of it was our personal weapons and some of it came from the Civilian Protection, from those who were on the reserve. Some of the weapons did arrive from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would people who were members of the guard receive uniforms and wear those uniforms while on guard?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Only those who had uniforms wore them. And those were members of the civilian protection. They had the so-called olive-drab green uniforms from Tito's time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber about how many people belonged and worked in this village guard?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: There were seven trenches and up to 30 men. There were three to four men in each of the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How many houses were in Bjelovac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: There were about 40 households, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be elaborating upon this section in a different manner. I think this might be a time period to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, right before we took a break, I asked you how many houses were in Bjelovac in 1992 and you testified that there were 40 households. You believe there were 40 households. How many of those households were Muslim households and how many of those households were Serb households?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: There were four Muslim households. The rest were Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did any of the Muslim households participate in the village guard?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Being a member of the village guard, did you receive any extra amenities, any extra clothing or food or money?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you also tell the Trial Chamber, in addition to the trenches that you testified about, what other places would the village guard stay and watch at night, in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: The border between Zaluzje and Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there any industrial sites in Bjelovac that were also guarded?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Only the water supply for Bratunac was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like you to take your time and describe to the Trial Chamber the layout of the town Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: It's a very small place. As I've already told you, there were 40 households or 40 houses in the area between Zaluzje and Sikirici, a kilometre and a half, maybe two kilometres of surface from close to the river Drina, and the river Drina is its border with the Republic of Serbia. So much for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour might I ask that I just lead the witness on this part of his evidence. It's about geographical placement and then I will be presenting a map for other things. I believe it would be in the best interests of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Also I'm saying go ahead, because I looked at the Defence and I saw Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic nodding, so I acknowledge their agreement to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Petrovic, is the town of Bjelovac located on the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Bjelovac is on the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And across from Bjelovac, do you have Serbia and, in particular, the Serbian city of Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Grabovica, Vrh Polje, those are the places in Serbia across the river Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is there a road that runs through Bjelovac and going toward the north, Zaluzje and eventually Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Zalazje? Or Zaluzje?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Zaluzje.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: That is the road to Bratunac. You go through Voljevica and you do arrive in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you take that same road in the opposite direction, going through Bjelovac, don't you arrive at Sikirici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sikirici and the -- then Tegare, Fakovici all the way up to Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, on one side of the road that cuts through Bjelovac, between the road and the Drina River, are there houses constructed where people in Bjelovac live?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: They are on both sides of the main road that passes through Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, on the side between the road and the river, there are houses that are constructed. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And on the other side of that road, there are houses that are constructed. And then after the houses, don't you have mountains or hills?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Hills. Hills are after the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the village guard had trenches and that they guarded the town from the trenches. Would you tell the Trial Chamber, were the trenches on the side of the road near the houses near the hills? Or on the other side of the road, the houses near the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: The trenches were below the hill, on the other side of the road. Not close to the river. At the foot of the hill they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would those posting guard, would they be guarding looking in the direction of the hills? Or would they be looking and guarding in the direction of the river?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the direction of the hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And why would they be guarding in that direction?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Because the Muslim forces could have arrived from that direction. There are the villages of Pirici and Poloznik there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you ever think that forces would be arriving from the other direction, from the direction of the river?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't expect that. We reckoned that Serbia was on that side, and the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to ask the usher to give Mr. Petrovic a map, because we've mentioned several places in the course of his testimony so far and I would just like to have that pointed out by him on a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very well, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like also to hand the usher a marker so he might be able to mark on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you've mentioned several places so far in your at the point. I would like to know, can you show the Trial Chamber where is Bjelovac on the map. And if you could mark it with, Your Honour, a small X or B, and then next to it your initials, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you also indicate for the Trial Chamber where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, but I would like you to put a circle around Bjelovac, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Please encircle Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now would you indicate for Your Honours where the Drina River is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he doesn't need to indicate that. We can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you now indicate for the Trial Chamber where Zaluzje is.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you do the same for Voljevica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And also for Bratunac, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you now please locate Sikirici and draw a circle around it also.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you also draw a circle around Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to draw a circle around Obadi, the town where you said that you -- the hamlet in which you were born.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just state for the record that the witness has drawn a circle around all of the places that we have named?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know whether you were finished or not. And at the same time I also want to ask, because the place where he put a circle now, at least trying to follow him on the map, I don't see Obadi written down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, is that the area where the town of Obadi is located, do you see the name?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't say that on the village. In any case, it is above Sase, above the lead and zinc mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Near -- well, so for the record, the witness has encircled all the towns and villages indicated to him by Madam Sellers during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I might also state, it might be self evident, where Srebrenica on the map, in relationship to these places. Could you indicate for us, Mr. Petrovic, where Srebrenica is, the town.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would ask that the map be given a number, but I would also ask that the map be kept near the witness because there will be a couple other places he will indicate in the course of his testimony and it might be easier if the map were there, he could turn to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Sellers. This map will be given Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P520. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just in case it might assist, we might have picked up on this any way, but Obadi is marked just with the letter, small spaced apart, above Gradina and above Sase. So it does actually appear, but it's -- as I say, the letters are spaced apart. Above Azlica you can see the "o," and then the "b," and the "a," and the "d," and the "i," just in case that helps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I am grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The"o" is just above Zalazje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you that the way it is spaced out on the map indicates a village. It indicates either an area, a region or a range of hills or mountains that are known by Obadi, by the name of Obadi. That recurs elsewhere in the -- on the map, on this and on others. Very rarely -- I don't even recall one instance where the name of a village is shown with letters spaced as they are on the spot which you have indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say that the village was indicated. Those words appear there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Okay. Thanks. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Petrovic, did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. I would like to continue now with the summer of 1992. Mr. Petrovic, I draw your attention to the fact that you have testified that there were village guards around the town of Bjelovac. Was Bjelovac attacked during the summer of 1992? And by that I mean June, July or August.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Bjelovac was attacked on the 14th of December, but in July the 28th of July, that was St Vitez's day, the village of Loznica, which is a bit further up from Bjelovac, was attacked. It is also a Serbian village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that July of 1992 or was that June of 1992 or another month that Loznica was attacked?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of July, that is the St Vitez's day, that is a Serbian Orthodox religious feast.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please, now on the map indicate for the Trial Chamber where is Loznica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has encircled on the map the place which he agrees to be Loznica, and this is along side the villages of Zalazje and Bjelovac and Voljevica. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, were you present in Loznica when the attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. I was in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you speak to anyone who was in Loznica when the attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. With those who had retreated from the village of Loznica, my neighbours from Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did they explain to you what they had observed and what had happened during that attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 28th of July, the they attacked Loznica and, during the day, all the houses were burnt down. The outcome of the fighting was eight people were killed and four people were wounded. I know some of them by name, if you want me to give them -- give you them, their names? All the houses were burned. And casualties were evacuated from the village, and nobody ever went back to Loznica itself, because the village was totally burned down and the guards continued to stand guard in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, was Loznica primarily a Bosnian Serb village or a Bosnian Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: A Serbian village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic you said that they attacked Loznica. Could you please tell me and tell the Trial Chamber who are you referring to when you say "they attacked"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Muslims. We knew some of them from Pirici Poznuk [phoen], and the neighbouring Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you say we knew some of them, does that mean that you recognised them? Or the persons who told you this recognised them? Or knew them by name?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: I did not recognise any of them because I was not up there, but this is what the people who were there, manning the positions in Loznica said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that they have come from the village of Pirici and from -- did you state the name of another village where the Muslim forces came from?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Pirici and Poloznik. These are the villages that border with Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are those predominantly Muslim villages or are they Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask you now to turn back to the map next to you and please indicate for the Trial Chamber where is Pirici and Poloznik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has encircled on the map the -- they mentioned two villages Pirici and Poloznik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic, still concentrating on the months of the summer of 1992, are you aware of any other village that was attacked in a similar manner?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the summer I think it was the 12th of June, St Peter's day, also a religious feast, the village of Obadi and Zalazje and another village were attacked. Obadi that's my home village, the place where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, were you present in the village of Obadi when it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I with a not. Two of my brothers, my father and my cousins were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you present in the village of Zalazje when it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did your brother -- brothers or your father tell you what happened during that attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: My brother told me. He was also a village guard in Obadi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what your brother told you about the attack on that day in Obadi.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the village of Zalazje, Azlica, and Obadi were attacked. At the same time, from the direction of Potocari and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, how was your brother able to see the attack occurring?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: He saw that because he was on the line guarding the village of Obadi and that's how he was able to observe the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did your brother indicate to you who attacked the village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: He said that the Muslims had attacked from the direction of Srebrenica and Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, what occurred during the attack, according to your brother?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the village was burnt on that day, the surviving villagers withdrew on that day, to the village of Andrici. That is the next village, the neighbouring village. My father and my brother, who is, how should I say that, a bit retarded, a little bit development problems, and his son, withdrew to Pobrdje to my father's sister.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour might I ask Mr. Petrovic to indicate, again, where the cities -- the towns or hamlets of Zaluzje and Azlica that he indicated in his testimony that were attacked on the day of Obadi. In the same day.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Not Zaluzje. But Zalazje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Zalazje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic, you indicated that the attackers were coming from the direction of Potocari. Would you also show that for the Trial Chamber on the map.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, the witness has indicated these three villages, that is Potocari, Zalazje and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Azlica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Azlica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did your brother tell you what time the attack began, what time of day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: The attack began in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was that in the morning before or after 10.00?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did the attack begin prior to it becoming light outside or did the attack begin after it was light, the sun had already rose in the sky?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the morning, when the day broke, the attack on Zalazje and Azlica began and then it spread to the village of Obadi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did your brother indicate or tell you about how many attackers were in the force that attacked the city?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he did not give me the exact figure, because he could not have done so. He just said that there were quite a few of them. He assumed between 300 to 500, maybe even 1000, because the attack covered a large territory. I don't know. He didn't give me the exact figure because he couldn't have known the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the houses were burned. Did your brother see who or how the houses were burned?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: All the houses were burned. We, as a family, had three houses in Obadi. All three of them were gutted by fire. In fact two were burned down to the stone foundations, and one was gutted by fire so that only the walls remained.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did your brother tell you whether the burning occurred due to mortar fire? Or any other means?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. It was -- fire was set to them. They were not burned by -- as a result of mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did your brother indicate who set the fire to the houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that it was Muslims. There was nobody else there. In fact there were only the two ethnic groups, Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In the attack of Loznica that you testified about earlier, you also indicated that houses were burned. Did you come to find out how the houses were burned?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the troops just went and set fire to them. The attackers, in fact, did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So therefore Mr. Petrovic, are you referring to the Muslim attackers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the three houses that your family owned in Obadi, were you ever compensated or reimbursed or given reparations by the attacking forces for that loss of property?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't get anything, and to this day nobody lives in that village. It's overgrown and there is nobody actually to return there. And we did not get any assistance to rebuild our houses. This is all now covered with vegetation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: After the attack in Loznica, were villagers able to move back into their town or their hamlet also?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. They were not able to go back there, because the village had been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any reparations or type of reimbursement in kind for the burnt houses in Loznica given to those inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. And to this day nobody lives in Loznica because they do not have the funds to rebuild their village, so nobody lives there in the village of Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, when we talk about the attack on Obadi, were there any persons who were captured or taken as prisoners as a result of that attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, from Obadi, no one. As from Zalazje, I heard people say that some people had been taken away. I don't know how many of them. I heard about Mijo Rakic and his brother, that they had been taken in the direction of either Srebrenica or Potocari. And that to this day their fate is unknown. They never reappeared. And the people who were up there said that some other people had been taken away, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now following the attack on Obadi, were there any presence of civilians in the area?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: After the attack on Obadi, after the Muslim forces attacked, were there civilians who came to the area?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please explain to the Trial Chamber what you learned about the civilians coming into the area after the attack on Obadi.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Muslim or Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, would you tell the Trial Chamber what happened if Muslim civilians came and also you can tell them what happened if Serb civilians came.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, Serbs used to live there. They couldn't have come there. Muslims, I guess, were just going there to loot the houses and burn them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did your brother tell you whether the houses that your family had in Obadi had been looted?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, everything was burnt down. The only thing we found in the -- in the newest house that was built of brick, we found the only -- the only thing that we found was a stove. But it was also burnt and damaged by fire. The rest of the -- the other two houses, because they were built the old way, nothing was left of them. They were burned down to the foundations. There were some barrels there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you testified that your fare and a nephew were in Obadi, but they were able to leave the village. Would you tell the Trial Chamber, how were they able to leave the village during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Not a cousin, but -- not a relative, but in fact two brothers, my father and a cousin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How were they able to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, they withdrew through the woods to Pobrdje, to my father's sister place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, had they received a warning that there would be an attack or did they just leave while the attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. In fact, the area where our houses were is a bit apart from the village, so they saw houses burning in the neighbouring village. They heard the shooting and they withdrew. My father was old. He was 72 years at the time. And my cousin was 16 years old at the time. One of my brothers was a bit retarded, and the younger brother, the second brother, he remained there to defend the village until they also retreated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you say they saw houses burning in the neighbouring village, just to be clear, what village are you speaking about? Which neighbouring village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Zalazje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to now stay within the summer of 1992 and refer you to one incident and that involves a nephew of yours. Did there come a time period when one of your nephews was taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He went there on his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Where did he go to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me explain. When he withdrew to Pobrdje, one day his aunt asked him to help her take her things to Bratunac. Since he was 16 years old, and he had never been to Bjelovac he left my aunt's stuff there, and my aunt went to Serbia by bus. And then, on his way back to Pobrdje because he didn't know the town, he headed towards Potocari. And so he went there, to their area in Potocari, and he stayed in Potocari for two months. We -- none of us knew where he was during that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you come to find out where he was eventually?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: We learned that when he was exchanged at Turbe. In fact it was the yellow bridge. Two months later we were told that he had been exchanged at the yellow bridge for some dead Serbs and Muslims [as interpreted]. I did not attend the exchange because that was not allowed and when he came to Bratunac, and when he was exchanged and when he came to the command to the headquarters, we were called and told that Slobodan Petrovic, that's my cousin's name, we were told that he had been released. We went to Bratunac to pick him up. We were not allowed to do so immediately in Bratunac. He was first taken to Zvornik to be interrogated. And then the next day, he was brought to Bjelovac, to my place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Just for the record unless it goes unnoticed. Line 18 on this page, 46, he had been exchanged at the yellow bridge for some dead Muslims it should be. Not some dead Serbs and Muslims. Some dead Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic when you indicated he had been exchanged for whom was he exchanged?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: He was brought to the checkpoint where the exchanges were taking place. In fact they brought the Serbs who had been killed in Srebrenica, in Zalazje, I don't know. I don't know whether the Muslims who had been exchanged were dead or alive, but there were some Muslims in the headquarters in Bratunac. They had been arrested and then they would be exchanged. Now, I don't know what this exchange involved. Dead Muslims or live Muslims. But about six or seven dead people, casualties were brought to be exchanged at that time, on a cart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, were you able to speak to your cousin about what had happened to him during the time period he was in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: We asked him, but since he was a bit retarded, it was hard for him to get some information. When we asked him where he was, he merely said that he slept in Potocari, below some concrete staircase. And of the names that we mentioned, he mentioned just one name, Naser. So later on, in Bjelovac, for the two or three months that he lived in Bjelovac before he was killed, everybody called him Naser. The Serbs in Bjelovac called him Naser because he had allegedly spent two or three months in Potocari, yet he never knew Naser because he lived in his village. He was a young boy. He probably must have heard that name from someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when your cousin came back, after being exchanged, would you tell the Trial Chamber in what state, what condition was his mouth?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in his upper jaw, he didn't have three of his teeth had been knocked out, when he came back. As for any other signs on his body, marks on his body, there weren't any. But since he did not want to talk about whether anyone had abused him or beat him, he never did tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, in fact there is a matter, Your Honour, which needs to be discussed in the absence of the -- of the witness, if he could be escorted out for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have the witness -- Mr. Petrovic, we need to discuss something which does not require your presence here. It doesn't concern you. But that's the -- that's precisely the reason why we would kindly ask you to be escorted, to leave the room a little bit, the courtroom. We will call you back when we finish discussing this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. This witness has just been giving detailed evidence firstly about attacks on Obadi, Zalazje, Azlica, which clearly -- the evidence clearly came as no surprise at all to the Prosecution. They had obviously proofed him on this subject and knew very well he was going to speak about these matters. More crucially than that, he has been talking about the detention of a Serb in Potocari, the name Naser has been mentioned, again some which clearly the Prosecution -- didn't take the Prosecution by surprise. And questions were being asked about his mouth, something very specific. Obviously which had been covered by the Prosecution with the witness in proofing. Now, we received proofing notes and they're about four paragraphs. There's no mention, certainly of any of these attacks on Obadi, Zalazje, or Azlica, and there is nothing about his cousin mentioning Naser, mistreatment possibly in Srebrenica, and this is pure ambush by the Prosecution against us. It's extremely unfair, because, in fact, if we receive no proofing notes, then we would be taken by surprise because this isn't in a witness statement, but we could at least put it to this witness. By providing us with proofing notes which omit, mention -- either the witness is going to mention Naser, that he is going to talk about detention charges, is actively misleading. I mean, it lulls us into -- into a sense of knowing what this witness is going to testify about, and then he comes along and testifies on something very different and gives evidence which may or may not be important. It may -- it may be that actually these matters regarding Naser ultimately aren't terribly important. But nonetheless, the Prosecution know that a witness is going to mention someone called Naser. He's going to talk about possible mistreatment in detention then we absolutely have a right to be notified about that in the proofing notes. Aside from the fact that ambush against the Defence is clearly prejudice shall to a fair trial and our rights, it also raises more basic issues of how this witness, the time with this witness is going to be managed, because we've all been very scrupulous to make sure that witnesses aren't kept over the weekend and whatnot, but if he -- if the witness is now going to give evidence, and we're hearing it for the first time, we may well not be able to finish with him tomorrow. We may need to go off and investigate further. We may need to consider our position, which, if we had received proofing notes which said he is going to mention these things, then we would have had time to think about it. So I can't imagine why the Prosecution omitted this information, which they clearly knew the witness was going to talk about, in the proofing notes. It's unacceptable in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have a look at the proofing notes, because we don't have them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I reply first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I take it, in due consideration, what counsel has said and in the statement that Defence counsel must have received from the 24th of May, 2000, he refers to the boy who was exchanged after being captured in the village Obadi about two months after the attack on the village. He had been kept for about two months in Potocari. This is an elaboration of that story. If counsel wants the proofing notes to actually be a stenographer's session, I do not believe that the Prosecution will comply with that. In terms of the other attacks that occurred during the summer, Your Honours, I will apologise, but this is just evidence of pattern that we're leading and I think it is well known there were attacks on several places. I did want to go directly to the statement where it said that, but I had no intention of all of ambushing the Defence. We're merely talking about attacks as pattern that are not charged in the indictment. I believe that is very clear and that we're trying, as a matter of fact, just to have the witness talk about what he has heard and what he knows. Now, if it is prejudicial to the point that the Defence has to prepare over the weekend or at a longer time period, certainly the Prosecution will not object to that. At the same time, I think that the nature of this witness's coming and trying to prepare this witness within the shortened proofing time, that those proofing notes were sent last night. If they should have been updated to the very least to say the name "Naser" will now be mentioned at another point in time, although we are aware that this witness was going to talk about Naser because he knew him from the days of the gas station, I would submit that the prejudice is of -- not quite as large as it offends counsel at this point is asserting. But if he needs more time to prepare on this incident, I don't think the Prosecution will object in any way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I might just reply. Obviously we don't ask for a stenographer's note, it is a position of what is clearly relevant and what clearly isn't. I mean, as for a mention of Naser, we have no idea how this boy heard the name Naser or if it refers to our client or to someone else and so I certainly don't wish to suggest there is any great forensic point in it. But the Prosecution has been keen to elicit that evidence of the name Naser. Keen to elicit something which happened with this witness's mouth to suggest mistreatment, all put together in close proximity, clearly an attempt to create an impression that somehow someone called Naser might be involved in the detention of this boy. If that is their case, then they absolutely need to puts on notice that that is evidence which they wish to elicit. And my learned friend was very keen to get that evidence. It was clear she was going straight for evidence which she knew the witness could give rather than alerting us to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your conclusion is a bit -- not a little bit but quite far fetched, trying to build it, sort of a jigsaw puzzle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. Really it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Given the timing, we were definitely not on the same wavelength on that. However, my concern is usual because you have both shown mutual respect and understanding in this. However, there is one vital point that I would like to make clear, that the three of us, that -- have been brought up and educated in a more or less traditional common law system - although I belong to a mixed system - are fully aware that the days where trials whereby ambush are dead and buried. It is no longer the case. It is finished. That belong two centuries ago. So I do share the concerns of Mr. Jones when he stands up and says: We thank you for having given us his prior statement. Thank you for having given us the proofing notes. But what you are asking him now and what he is answering - which is of no surprise to you - is indicative that these items were on the agenda, were on the menu, but they were unwritten. And we all of a sudden find ourselves faced with these issue. Don't expect me to comment on whether the issues that have been raised by Mr. Jones are serious, less serious, or insignificant. That's something on which neither I, nor my colleagues will certainly comment. But the fact that issues -- or facts are mentioned during the testimony in a way which clearly indicates that they were anticipated, irritates a little bit. Irritates, in the sense that I don't think we can tolerate it. So the remedy that you suggest, all right, Your Honours, if for further sake the Defence needs time to prepare for Defence and so on and so forth, it is no justification. I mean, it is a solution which would redress the injustice that might have been occasioned otherwise, but in reality it shouldn't be like that. Why should we keep this witness an extra two days over the week he had plus an extra day or two until he finishes his testimony and then return simply because the Rules have not been adhered to? So at this time I leave all options open. I definitely am not going to tell the Defence cases -- matter is closed. We don't visit it again. I don't know, because I don't know what the witness is going to continue saying. I don't know what can be covered in cross-examination and whether it can be covered in cross-examination by tomorrow. So I don't know. But these incidents should be avoided at all costs. And I think it is a question of loyalty amongst yourselves and, together, and separately, loyalty towards the Bench. Very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not accusing you of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to say just for practical purposes I was about to conclude that line with just asking him, in terms of the oral hygiene. I will drop that line of questioning, but also would like to emphasize to the Defence that none of that was done in bad faith. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. I am pretty sure it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But we will continue with a different line of questioning, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it wasn't. Don't take my words as attacking you or censoring you, but to an extent I am, because I am making it clear that trials by ambush are not within the agenda of this Tribunal. So we will not tolerate it. But I think we can proceed now. Madam Usher, please. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Thank you, Mr. Petrovic for being patient with us. We have solved the problem that we had, something that doesn't concern you. It concerns Prosecution and Defence and the relation between them. So I think that, having been cleared, Ms. Sellers can --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I beg your indulgence for four minutes and ask the witness to leave again. There is something I think that I should just relate to state on the record within --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think you have to leave the room again. I'm sorry about this, but these accidents do happen and certain matters, yes, cannot be discussed in the presence of the witness, according to the Rules. I'm sorry about this, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much. I just do want to state for the record that this line of questioning we were discussing procedurally, I just wanted to state substantively this line of questioning went to the credibility of another witness who has spoken Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about this person who was kept in Potocari and I felt I was leading this certainly not as a surprise, but to bolster the testimony of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I mean, I do not --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I just want to state that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, I do not question the good intentions and the expertise that lay behind your line of questions. The question that arises is, whether the Defence ought to have been put on notice. Because it does not arise -- this matter does not arise from his statement. I mean, these details. I know that this matter was mentioned by another witness. I mean, that much I recall. And I put two and two together, because you precisely asked these questions now. But I wasn't expecting these questions, because I hadn't seen the proofing notes. But had I seen the proofing notes, I still would not have expected those questions to be put. I'm pretty sure that Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser are of the same opinion, share the same opinion with me, as you see, I mean we cannot stop and discuss every single matter, but if they disagree with me, please say so. And on that score, I cannot but agree with Mr. Jones. I mean he was taken by surprise. They were taken by surprise, and they shouldn't be taken by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, it is no big deal if we are taken by surprise because we have got a thicker skin, but the Defence cannot be taken by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not using the word "ambush."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I do agree with you. I just wanted to state that for the record the purpose of that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It still doesn't justify.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I completely understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, it's not simply this boy, that evidence which is new. Loznica burning and looting also is entirely new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Jones, let's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The reason I mention is it is outside the indictment but if we're to cross examine properly it is actually no small matter to cross examine about what happened in an attack on a village. It's non-trivial. And if it is something with which is outside of the indictment and we can disregard it, that is one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. Agreed. On the other hand when you're a judge and you're presiding over a trial, if you try to direct every bit of evidence, every question, every answer, exclusively to what is contained in the indictment, each testimony will last twice as long. It will become coordinated, full of interruptions. We adopt the same system with you, many questions that you ask relate to events that have got nothing to do with the indictment, pre and post. And it's not a question of closing our eyes. It is a question of trial experience and trial technique. It's -- there may be hidden reasons that you discover as you go along and that you wouldn't want to anticipate or pre-empt not knowing what the relevance would be. So I would like you to understand that we adopt a system of trial here that should not allow place for surprises. That's all. I mean it is -- no party should be surprised by the other. If there is such surprises, then obviously there will be a remedy provided for by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. May I just, in that respect, Your Honour, enquire whether, if an attack -- say characterised by the Prosecution is mentioned which is outside the indictment and we don't -- no, Your Honour, I'm perhaps going to make a different one from the one that Your Honour anticipates. If in the interests of an expeditious trial we don't cross examine fully on that matter because it is outside the indictment, I take it then from what Your Honours said, the Bench is not going to later take that we admitted in any part that evidence. It is simply outside the indictment and therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Jones. Let's make it clear. You know that there is such a thing as a system of conduct. That is sometimes sought to be proven by the Prosecution, by means of reference to events that are not the events included in the indictment. Such questions and such references are allowed and we certainly don't stop them. The relevance can be put to -- or asked, and well if you ask the question, that's the answer you are going to get. This is -- we're trying to prove that, the system of attacks was similar or identical or standard throughout, even -- not only in the places included in the indictment, but all around. All right. So, et cetera. So your interest is only insofar as it seeks to prove a system of conduct. You should not, at any moment, be bothered with ourselves being bothered with those particular attacks that are not in reality part of the indictment. If your client, at the end of the day, is going to be found guilty, he will be found guilty of what is contained in the indictment. He will not be found guilty or his responsibility will not increase because we have heard, in the course of the trial, that it wasn't only three, four, five villages that were attacked, but there were another sixty villages that were attacked, and ransacked, and burned down by the Muslim forces under his control or not under his control. To us, we allow it during the hearing of the testimony, but it's not going to influence us. Insofar as it seeks to a prove system of conduct, it may be relevant. So there it is up to you what stand to take in relation to that type of -- kind of testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour. It's just -- that's precisely it. It is -- this evidence is being adduced to prove a system of conduct and therefore we of course have to be in a position to cross examine to show that no such system existed and therefore we do need to be notified if these villages, additional villages are going to be mentioned. It's simply to make that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, I agree with you. Because there is no other -- I mean, if there is any other reason that I'm not aware of, please, Ms. Sellers, do tell me. But I see no other reason why time is being spent with this witness to relate to us the events that took place in villages during attacks that are not included in the indictment. There must be a reason, obviously. I mean you haven't stood up and said "objection, what's the relevance of the question". In the back of our mind, you know now what we think. I mean, the only relevance that there could be is precisely a system of conduct which could relate to various matters, but a system of conduct essentially. The same applies to this boy who was -- I don't know if he was imprisoned, not imprisoned, because the witness was laconic there. But again it would show a system of conduct of keeping prisoners and then exchanging them, for example. So therefore I agree 100 percent with you, that if these matters are going to be raised during the examination-in-chief, you should be given prior notice of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I think that is the basic principle which we needed to establish and that is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can take it for granted that that is the case, but we are not always in a position to anticipate it. First, because in the normality of cases we are not given copies of the proofing notes. Secondly, because I, for one, am -- rarely choose to go through the statements before I come here to hear the testimony. I do check when it's going on. And I do check before to see more or less what the testimony is going to cover. But I don't normally go through the details. So at the end of the day, I don't -- and there are very few questions that I can anticipate. I mean, if I see that this person was one of the prisoners in Srebrenica, then obviously I know that I can expect questions on the attack, how he or she were captured, questions relating to detention, questions relating to exchange and so on and so forth. Not beyond that. Especially if there are other -- other matters covered, that of course I wouldn't know about. I don't mind being taken by surprise, because the cases -- and not mine as such. But I will make sure that you will not be taken by surprise. All right. So, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the position is as follows:

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can bring in the witness now, please. And your position is as follows, Mr. Jones. Your position is reserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I should say it is my colleague who will be cross-examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it us it doesn't make a difference whether it is you or your colleague. You are the Defence team, together. So when I say "your position," I don't mean yours. I mean the accused's position, basically. It is reserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will hear any submissions you may have in that regard later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We may need to be prepared to go on to Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, if that is a possibility, I mean we will have -- I'm certainly not going to tell you "No, I have decided on the basis of what we discussed yesterday, that there will not be a sitting on Monday," that this person will go back on Friday. If things happen the way they did and we need to keep him here and continue with him Monday, then we continue with him on Monday.
